summary: This Best Current Practice describes the IETF Administrative Support Activity, set up inside the Internet Society. It defines the roles of the IETF Administrative Oversight Committee, the IETF Administrative Director, and ISOC in the IETF's administration. It was replaced by RFC 8711.

plainLanguage.summary: The IETF needs people to handle money, contracts and office tasks. This document explains who does what in that support team. It was later replaced by RFC 8711.

questions: who is the ietf administrative director
subtitle: How the IETF's administrative and financial operations are organized and overseen.

tldr.problem: The IETF needed an organization to handle administrative and financial tasks that support the standards process, separate from technical decision-making.
tldr.mechanism: The IETF Administrative Support Activity (IASA) is housed within the Internet Society, led by an IETF Administrative Director (IAD) managed by an IETF Administrative Oversight Committee (IAOC).
tldr.outcome: The IASA provides structure to collect meeting fees, manage contracts, handle finances and budgets, and support IETF technical activities, while keeping administrative decisions separate from standards development.

facts.label: IASA funding sources
facts.value: 3 sources: meeting revenues, donations, ISOC support

facts.label: Operating reserve
facts.value: 6 months of operating expenses plus meeting guarantees

today: RFC 4071 was made obsolete by RFC 8711 in August 2013. RFC 8711 updated the structure to create a single IETF Administrative Director and reorganized the administrative structure, while maintaining the principle of separating IETF technical decisions from administrative operations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 4071 defines the structure of the IETF Administrative Support Activity (IASA), which handles all the non-technical administrative and financial work needed to run the IETF. This is a formal Best Current Practice document that spells out who does what, how money flows, and how oversight works.

The IASA is deliberately kept separate from the IETF's technical work. The IETF makes decisions on protocols and standards through consensus and the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG). The IASA handles money, contracts, facilities and other administrative needs. The two are carefully separated so that administrative decisions never influence technical ones.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF group sits down to write Internet standards. They need a separate team to handle money and paperwork so the technical people can focus on good standards.

sections.title: The IASA Structure
sections.content:
The IASA is housed inside the Internet Society (ISOC), which is a non-profit organization. It consists of a single full-time employee, the IETF Administrative Director (IAD), who manages the day-to-day work and reports to a committee called the IETF Administrative Oversight Committee (IAOC).

The IAOC is made up of eight voting members selected in different ways: two appointed by the IETF Nominations Committee, one each from the IESG and IAB, one from the ISOC Board of Trustees, plus three ex officio members (the IETF Chair, IAB Chair, and ISOC President). The IAD also sits on the IAOC as a non-voting member.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one person called the IAD who handles the IASA's work. A committee of eight people watches what the IAD does and tells them what to do. Some of the committee members come from the IETF technical groups, some from ISOC.

sections.title: What the IAD and IAOC Do
sections.content:
The IAD manages contracts with service providers (such as organizations that run IETF meetings or manage documents), handles all IETF finances, administers the budget, and ensures that money and resources are spent wisely. The IAD also makes sure that IETF intellectual property (like domain names and copyrights) is protected.

The IAOC does not do the day-to-day work. Instead, it sets direction, reviews the IAD's plans and reports, ensures that IETF administrative needs are met, approves budgets and major contracts, and holds the IAD accountable. If a community member believes the IAOC made a wrong decision, they can ask for a formal review, and if they are not satisfied, they can appeal to the IAB or ISOC Board of Trustees.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAD is like the manager who pays the bills and makes contracts. The IAOC is the bosses who check that the manager is doing a good job and not spending too much money.

sections.title: Money and Budget
sections.content:
The IASA gets money from three sources: revenues from IETF meetings (registration fees), donations to ISOC that are designated for the IETF, and other support from ISOC. The IAD, working with the IAOC, sets the budget each year and submits it to the ISOC Board of Trustees for approval.

All IETF money and spending must be tracked separately and reported publicly. The IASA is expected to keep a financial reserve sufficient to cover six months of operating costs, so that the IETF can stay open even if unexpected events reduce income.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF gets money from people who come to meetings, from people who donate, and from ISOC. Every year they plan how much money they need and what it will be spent on. They keep some money in savings in case of emergencies.

sections.title: Keeping Power in Check
sections.content:
The document is very careful to ensure that nobody gets too much power. The IAOC must communicate regularly with the IETF community and hold open meetings at IETF meetings at least once a year. The IAD and IAOC must publish monthly, quarterly and annual financial and operational reports.

If the IASA is ever moved from ISOC to a different organization, all contracts must allow the move to happen with at least six months' notice. The idea is that the IASA belongs to the IETF community, not to ISOC.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAD and IAOC tell everyone what they are doing with the money every month. If the community does not like their decisions, they can speak up. The IASA was set up so it can move to a different organization if the IETF needs it to.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: RFC 4071 was replaced by RFC 8711, which updates the structure of the IASA as the IETF continued to grow and administrative needs evolved. However, the core principles and structure defined in RFC 4071 established how the IETF's administrative function is organized and overseen.
sections.plainLanguage: This document was updated by RFC 8711 because the IETF got bigger and needed some changes. But the basic idea — a manager and a committee watching the manager — stayed the same.
